title: Entra ID (Azure AD) + RBAC -- the identity and access model
exp: Azure's access model maps onto IAM conceptually but is expressed through Role-Based Access Control assigned at points in the resource hierarchy from Day 1, rather than JSON policy documents attached to users.
pts: Entra ID (formerly Azure AD): the identity provider behind every login, service principal, and Managed Identity -- the Azure equivalent of IAM's user/role identity layer.

RBAC role assignment = (security principal) + (role definition) + (scope). Scope can be Management Group, Subscription, Resource Group, or a single Resource -- narrower scope always applies in addition to broader ones.

Built-in roles: Reader (view only), Contributor (full read/write/delete, cannot grant access to others), Owner (Contributor + can grant roles). Prefer built-in roles over custom roles unless there's a genuine gap.

Managed Identity: Azure's answer to an EC2 instance profile -- a service gets an identity with no secrets to manage, auto-rotated credentials. System-assigned ties to one resource's lifecycle; user-assigned is standalone and shareable across services.

Service Principal: an app-level identity used for CI/CD or automation that isn't tied to a specific resource's lifecycle -- roughly the Azure equivalent of an IAM user created specifically for programmatic access.

Azure Policy enforces organization-wide rules (like 'only allow resources in these regions') independent of RBAC -- RBAC controls WHO can do WHAT, Policy controls WHAT is allowed to exist at all, regardless of who's doing it.
code:
# RBAC assignment -- scope to the resource group, not the whole subscription
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <managed-identity-object-id> \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-orders-pipeline/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/satishpipeline"

# Create a Managed Identity for a service (e.g. a Databricks workspace)
az identity create --name id-orders-pipeline --resource-group rg-orders-pipeline

# Azure Policy -- deny resource creation outside approved regions
az policy assignment create \
  --name "restrict-to-eu-regions" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<sub-id>" \
  --policy "location-restriction-policy-id" \
  --params '{"listOfAllowedLocations":{"value":["westeurope","northeurope"]}}'

qa.q: What is the Azure equivalent of an AWS IAM instance role, and what's the one meaningful naming distinction to know?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Managed Identity. System-assigned Managed Identity is tied to a single resource's lifecycle (created and destroyed with it) -- the closer analog to an EC2 instance profile. User-assigned Managed Identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to multiple services at once and outlives any single resource -- useful when several services need the same permission set, which has no single clean AWS equivalent since instance profiles are inherently per-instance.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Cloud control plane APIs orchestrate virtualized hardware, networking (VPC/VNets), IAM policies, and auto-scaling groups.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Overly permissive IAM roles (wildcard actions) or unmonitored resource limits lead to security breaches and unexpected cloud cost spikes.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Serverless/managed services eliminate infrastructure maintenance but introduce cold starts and vendor lock-in.

qa.q: What's the difference between RBAC and Azure Policy, and why do interviewers ask this specifically?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** RBAC controls WHO can perform WHAT actions on WHICH resources -- it's an access control layer. Azure Policy controls WHAT is allowed to exist or be configured at all, regardless of who's attempting it -- e.g. 'no resource may be created outside EU regions,' enforced even against someone who otherwise has full Owner rights. Interviewers ask this because conflating the two is a common real mistake -- someone assumes an RBAC restriction also enforces a compliance rule like data residency, when that actually requires Policy.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Cloud control plane APIs orchestrate virtualized hardware, networking (VPC/VNets), IAM policies, and auto-scaling groups.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Overly permissive IAM roles (wildcard actions) or unmonitored resource limits lead to security breaches and unexpected cloud cost spikes.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Serverless/managed services eliminate infrastructure maintenance but introduce cold starts and vendor lock-in.

qa.q: Why would you use a Service Principal instead of a Managed Identity for a CI/CD pipeline?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Managed Identity is tied to an actual Azure resource running the workload (a VM, a Function App) -- it doesn't exist independent of that resource. A CI/CD pipeline running outside Azure (on GitHub Actions runners, for instance) has no Azure resource to attach a Managed Identity to, so it needs a Service Principal -- an app-level identity that exists independently and can authenticate from anywhere, ideally via Workload Identity Federation so no long-lived secret needs to be stored.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Cloud control plane APIs orchestrate virtualized hardware, networking (VPC/VNets), IAM policies, and auto-scaling groups.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Overly permissive IAM roles (wildcard actions) or unmonitored resource limits lead to security breaches and unexpected cloud cost spikes.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Serverless/managed services eliminate infrastructure maintenance but introduce cold starts and vendor lock-in.

interviewPlaybook.openingScript: In enterprise cloud environments, Entra ID (Azure AD) + RBAC -- the identity and access model must be designed with fault tolerance, zero-downtime deployment pipelines, and explicit security boundaries.
interviewPlaybook.incidentStory: A regional outage threatened pipeline ingestion availability when a dependency failed around Entra ID (Azure AD) + RBAC -- the identity and access model. Using infrastructure-as-code and automated failover, I implemented circuit breaking and fallback routing, keeping client payload ingestion at 99.99% availability.
whiteboardSteps: 1. Ingress Cloud Load Balancer / API Gateway → IAM Authentication
2. Managed Compute (Container / Function) → Orchestration of Entra ID (Azure AD) + RBAC -- the identity and access model
3. Persistent Storage / Event Bus (Kafka/S3/DB) → Partitioning & Replication
